ASSURED SHORTHOLD TENANCY AGREEMENT

This agreement is made on 18 January 2024 between Greenfield Lettings Ltd, acting as agent for the owner Mr Howard Pemberton (together called the Landlord), whose office is at Unit 4, Mercer Court, Ashbourne Vale AV1 2BX, and Ms Maya Collins and Mr Daniel Reyes (together called the Tenants). Where there is more than one Tenant, each is jointly and severally responsible for every obligation in this agreement.

1. THE PROPERTY

The Landlord lets to the Tenants the residential flat known as Flat 3, 14 Larkspur Row, Ashbourne Vale AV3 9QT, together with the use of the shared entrance hall, stairs, bin store and the allocated parking bay numbered 3 at the rear of the building. The fixtures, fittings and furniture listed in the attached inventory are included. The garden area to the front of the building remains under the control of the Landlord and may be used by all occupiers for quiet enjoyment only.

2. THE TERM

The tenancy begins on 1 February 2024 and runs for a fixed term of twelve months, ending on 31 January 2025. If neither party gives notice and the Tenants remain in occupation after the fixed term, the tenancy will continue as a periodic tenancy on the same conditions, with the rental period running from the first day of each calendar period.

3. RENT

The rent is £1,150 per calendar month, due in advance on the first day of each rental period. The first instalment of £1,150 must be received in cleared funds before the keys are released. Subsequent instalments are to be transferred by standing order to the client account of Greenfield Lettings Ltd, sort code 00-00-00, account number 00012345, quoting the reference LARK3. If any rent is more than fourteen days late, the Landlord may charge interest at 3 percent above the Bank of England base rate, calculated daily from the date the rent was due until it is received.

The Landlord may propose a rent review no earlier than the end of the fixed term, by giving at least one month of written notice. Any increase must be reasonable and in line with the local market for comparable homes.

4. DEPOSIT

The Tenants shall hand over a deposit of £1,327 on or before the signing of this agreement. The deposit will be protected with the SafeHold Deposit Scheme within thirty days of receipt, and the prescribed information will be given to the Tenants within the same period. At the end of the tenancy the deposit will be returned within ten days of both parties agreeing the amount, less any reasonable deductions for unpaid rent, damage beyond fair wear and tear, missing items from the inventory, or cleaning required to return the Property to the condition recorded at check-in. Any dispute about deductions may be referred free of charge to the adjudication service of the scheme.

5. UTILITIES AND COUNCIL TAX

The Tenants are responsible for gas, electricity, water, telephone, broadband, the television licence and council tax for the Property during the tenancy. The Tenants must notify each supplier and the local council of the start and end dates of the tenancy and must take meter readings on moving in and moving out. The Tenants must not change the supplier of any utility in a way that requires alterations to the meters or wiring without the written consent of the Landlord, which will not be unreasonably withheld.

6. TENANT OBLIGATIONS

The Tenants agree to keep the interior of the Property clean and in good decorative order, allowing for fair wear and tear; to take reasonable care of the fixtures, fittings and furniture; to replace light bulbs, fuses and smoke alarm batteries when needed; to keep the drains, sinks and toilets free from blockages caused by misuse; to ventilate the Property adequately to prevent condensation and mould, including the use of extractor fans when cooking or bathing; to report any disrepair or defect to the Landlord promptly in writing; and to make sure the Property is left secure, with all windows closed and doors locked, whenever it is unoccupied.

The Tenants must not cause a nuisance or annoyance to neighbours or other occupiers of the building; must not play amplified music so loudly that it can be heard outside the Property between 11pm and 7am; must not smoke or allow visitors to smoke inside the Property; must not use the Property for any business that involves visiting customers; and must not keep any dangerous or flammable materials other than ordinary household products.

The Tenants must not make any alterations or additions to the Property, including painting, putting up shelves, changing locks or installing satellite dishes, without the prior written consent of the Landlord. Small picture hooks may be used, provided any holes are neatly filled at the end of the tenancy.

7. LANDLORD OBLIGATIONS

The Landlord agrees to allow the Tenants quiet enjoyment of the Property without interruption; to keep in repair the structure and exterior of the Property, including drains, gutters and external pipes; to keep in repair and proper working order the installations for the supply of water, gas, electricity, sanitation, space heating and hot water; to arrange an annual gas safety check by a registered technician and provide a copy of the certificate to the Tenants; to provide a valid Energy Performance Certificate and an Electrical Installation Condition Report; and to insure the building against fire and other usual risks. The Landlord's insurance does not cover the Tenants' own belongings, and the Tenants are advised to arrange their own contents insurance.

8. REPAIRS AND EMERGENCIES

Non-urgent repairs should be reported through the Greenfield Lettings online portal or by email to maintenance@greenfield-lettings.example. In an emergency, such as a major water leak, total loss of heating in winter, a gas smell or an electrical hazard, the Tenants should call the out-of-hours line on 0000 000 0000. The Landlord will aim to attend emergencies within 24 hours and routine repairs within 14 days.

9. ACCESS

The Tenants shall allow the Landlord, the agent or contractors access to the Property at reasonable times of the day to inspect its condition or carry out repairs, provided at least 24 hours of written notice is given, except in an emergency when immediate access may be needed. During the last two months of the tenancy, the Tenants shall allow viewings by prospective tenants or buyers at reasonable times by prior arrangement.

10. PETS

The Tenants must not keep any animal at the Property without the prior written consent of the Landlord. The Landlord has given consent for the Tenants to keep one small dog, namely a cockapoo called Biscuit, on condition that the dog is not left alone in the Property for more than six hours at a time, that any fouling in the shared areas or the front garden is cleared immediately, and that the Tenants arrange professional cleaning of carpets and flea treatment of the Property at the end of the tenancy. No other animals may be kept without further written consent, and consent may be withdrawn if the dog causes a nuisance to neighbours.

11. SUBLETTING AND ASSIGNMENT

The Tenants must not assign, sublet, take in lodgers or part with possession of the whole or any part of the Property. Short-term holiday letting through any online platform is strictly prohibited. Overnight guests are permitted for no more than fourteen nights in any rolling three-month period.

12. BREAK CLAUSE

Either party may end the tenancy early by giving at least two months of written notice, provided that the notice does not expire before 31 July 2024, which is the end of the sixth month of the fixed term. Rent will be due up to the date the notice expires. If the Tenants wish to leave before that date, they may ask the Landlord to agree a surrender, and the Landlord may require the Tenants to cover reasonable re-letting costs, capped at £300 plus VAT.

13. ENDING THE TENANCY

At the end of the tenancy the Tenants must return all keys, remove all their belongings and rubbish, and leave the Property in the same clean condition recorded in the inventory, allowing for fair wear and tear. A check-out inspection will be carried out by an independent inventory clerk, and the Tenants are welcome to attend. Any items left behind after the Tenants have gone may be disposed of after fourteen days.

14. NOTICES

Under section 48 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1987, the Tenants are notified that notices, including notices in proceedings, may be served on the Landlord at the office of Greenfield Lettings Ltd given above. Notices to the Tenants may be delivered by hand to the Property, by first class post or by email to the addresses given on the signature page.

15. INVENTORY SUMMARY

Living room: grey two-seater sofa, oak coffee table, floor lamp, cream curtains. Bedroom 1: double bed frame with mattress, wardrobe, two bedside tables. Bedroom 2: single bed, small desk. Kitchen: fridge freezer, washing machine, electric oven and hob, extractor hood, kettle. Bathroom: mirror cabinet, shower screen. Meter readings at check-in: electricity 48213, gas 10392, water 00771.

Signed for the Landlord: R. Ashworth, Lettings Manager, Greenfield Lettings Ltd.
Signed by the Tenants: Maya Collins, Daniel Reyes.
Date: 18 January 2024.

docs.name: Home insurance policy.txt
docs.body:
HEARTHSAFE HOME INSURANCE
CONTENTS INSURANCE POLICY WORDING AND SCHEDULE

Policyholder: Maya Collins and Daniel Reyes
Policy number: HS-CNT-0049921
Insured address: Flat 3, 14 Larkspur Row, Ashbourne Vale AV3 9QT
Period of insurance: 1 February 2024 to 31 January 2025
Type of cover: Contents only, with accidental damage and personal possessions extensions
Sum insured for contents: £35,000
Personal possessions away from the home: £2,500, single item limit £1,000

SECTION A: ABOUT THIS POLICY

This policy is a contract between you and Hearthsafe Home Insurance. It is based on the information you gave us when you took out the policy. Please read the schedule and this wording together, because the schedule shows which sections you have chosen and any special conditions that apply to you. If any of the information you gave us is wrong or has changed, please tell us as soon as possible, because it may affect your cover or the price.

We will insure you during the period of insurance for loss or damage described in the sections you have chosen, provided you have paid the premium and you keep to the conditions of this policy.

SECTION B: DEFINITIONS

Contents means household goods, furniture, carpets, clothing, electronic devices, valuables and personal belongings which you own or are legally responsible for, kept in the home. Contents does not include motor vehicles, caravans, boats, money above £500, deeds and bonds, animals, or any part of the structure of the building.

Valuables means jewellery, watches, items of gold, silver or other precious metals, pictures and works of art, and collections of stamps, coins or medals.

The home means the private flat at the insured address, together with any lockable outbuildings used for domestic purposes.

Unoccupied means not lived in by you or a member of your family for more than 60 consecutive days.

SECTION C: WHAT IS COVERED

1. Fire, smoke, explosion, lightning and earthquake.
2. Storm and flood, but not damage to gates, fences or hedges, and not damage caused by frost.
3. Escape of water from any fixed water installation, washing machine, dishwasher or fish tank.
4. Escape of oil from any fixed heating installation.
5. Theft or attempted theft, provided there has been forced and violent entry or exit if the home is lent, let or sublet.
6. Riot, civil commotion, strikes and labour disturbances.
7. Malicious damage or vandalism.
8. Collision by aircraft, vehicles or animals.
9. Falling trees, branches, aerials, satellite dishes and masts.
10. Subsidence, heave or landslip.

ACCIDENTAL DAMAGE EXTENSION
We will cover accidental damage to your contents in the home. Examples include spilling paint on a carpet, dropping a television, or breaking a glass table top. We will not cover damage caused by pets chewing, scratching or fouling, damage to clothing while being worn, or damage to mobile phones, which are covered only under the personal possessions section.

PERSONAL POSSESSIONS EXTENSION
We will cover your personal possessions, such as handbags, phones, laptops, jewellery and spectacles, against loss, theft or damage anywhere in the world for up to 60 days in any period of insurance. Pedal cycles are covered up to £600 each if locked to an immovable object when left unattended.

SECTION D: ADDITIONAL COVERS INCLUDED AT NO EXTRA COST

Alternative accommodation: if your home cannot be lived in because of damage covered by this policy, we will pay reasonable costs of alternative accommodation for you, your family and your pets, up to 20 percent of the contents sum insured.

Freezer contents: up to £400 for food spoiled because of a rise or fall in temperature.

Replacement locks: up to £500 to replace locks to external doors if keys are lost or stolen.

Students' belongings: up to £3,000 for contents belonging to a family member studying away from home.

Tenant's liability: up to £10,000 for damage to the landlord's fixtures and fittings for which you are legally liable as a tenant.

Garden contents: up to £1,000 for plants, furniture and ornaments in the open, but not against storm or flood.

SECTION E: WHAT IS NOT COVERED

Wear and tear, gradual deterioration, moth or vermin damage, mechanical or electrical breakdown, and any loss of value after a repair. Loss or damage while the home is unoccupied, other than fire, lightning and explosion. Theft by people you have lawfully allowed into the home, unless forced entry was used. Any loss caused deliberately by you or by someone living with you. Damage caused by faulty workmanship, design or materials.

SECTION F: EXCESSES

The excess is the first part of any claim that you must contribute. The standard excess for each claim under this policy is £100. For claims for escape of water from any installation, washing machine or dishwasher, the excess is £350. For subsidence claims the excess is £1,000. A voluntary excess of £50 applies in addition to the standard excess, in return for the discount shown on your schedule. Where a single incident gives rise to claims under more than one section, only the highest excess will be applied.

SECTION G: HOW WE SETTLE CLAIMS

We will replace items as new, apart from clothing and household linen, for which we will make a deduction for wear and tear. We may choose to repair the item, replace it, or offer a cash settlement equal to what it would cost us to replace it through our suppliers. If the sum insured is less than the full replacement cost of all your contents at the time of the loss, we may reduce any claim payment in proportion.

SECTION H: CONDITIONS

You must take all reasonable steps to prevent loss or damage and keep your property in good condition. You must lock all external doors and close all windows when the home is left empty. You must tell us within 30 days about any change of address, any change in the number of people living at the home, or if you start running a business from it. You must report any theft or malicious damage to the police within 24 hours and obtain a crime reference number. You must not admit liability or make any offer to settle a claim without our written consent.

SECTION I: MAKING A CLAIM

Contact the Hearthsafe claims team as soon as possible on the number shown in your welcome pack, or report your claim online at any time. Keep damaged items until we have had the opportunity to inspect them, and take photographs where you can. We may ask for receipts, bank statements, valuations or photographs as proof of ownership and value.

SECTION J: CANCELLATION

You may cancel within 14 days of receiving this policy and we will refund the premium in full, provided no claim has been made. After that, you may cancel at any time and we will refund a proportionate share of the premium, less a £25 administration fee.

SECTION K: COMPLAINTS

If you are unhappy with our service, please contact our customer relations team in the first instance. If we cannot resolve your complaint within eight weeks, you may refer it to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which is free to use.

SCHEDULE SUMMARY
Annual premium: £148.20 including Insurance Premium Tax
No claims discount: 3 years
Specified valuables: engagement ring, £1,800; Kalden digital camera, £650
Special condition: the front door must be fitted with a five-lever mortice deadlock.

SECTION L: LEGAL EXPENSES (OPTIONAL, NOT SELECTED)

Legal expenses cover was offered at renewal for £24 a year and was declined. This means the policy does not fund solicitors' fees in disputes with employers, neighbours, landlords or suppliers. A free legal helpline is still available to all policyholders for general advice, open from 9am to 5pm on weekdays.

SECTION M: HOME EMERGENCY (OPTIONAL, NOT SELECTED)

Home emergency cover for boiler breakdown, plumbing and drainage, and lost keys was also offered and declined, because the landlord is responsible for the boiler and the main water and drainage systems under the tenancy agreement.

SECTION N: HOW YOUR PERSONAL INFORMATION IS USED

docs.name: Project report - Tidewell churn analysis.md
docs.body:
# Tidewell Telecom: Customer Churn Analysis
Final report, prepared by Maya Collins and Owen Pike, Lumen Analytics Ltd
Version 1.3, 12 September 2024

## 1. Executive overview

Tidewell Telecom asked Lumen Analytics to understand why residential broadband and mobile customers leave, to estimate which customers are most at risk, and to recommend practical actions for the retention team. This report covers twenty-four months of account data from July 2022 to June 2024, covering about 410,000 residential accounts across the south west and the midlands. It describes the data we used, our methods, the findings, and our recommendations, together with an outline of the experiment we propose for the fourth quarter.

Overall annual churn across the period was 17.8 percent, higher than the 14 percent target that Tidewell set in its 2023 business plan. Churn was concentrated in customers who had come to the end of their minimum term, in customers on older copper broadband products, and in customers who had contacted the support line three or more times in the previous ninety days.

## 2. Background and scope

Tidewell is a regional provider with a strong reputation for local service but limited marketing budget compared with national competitors. In 2023 it moved most of its residential base onto a new billing platform, which changed how renewals and price rises are presented on statements. The retention team had noticed an increase in cancellation calls after the migration but did not have a clear picture of the causes or of which customer groups were driving the trend.

The scope agreed in the statement of work was: a descriptive analysis of churn by segment; a predictive model of churn risk at account level, refreshed monthly; an analysis of the reasons customers give when they cancel; and a short list of recommended interventions with expected impact. Business customers and prepaid mobile customers were out of scope.

## 3. Data sources

We used five data sources supplied by Tidewell under the data sharing agreement signed in May 2024:

1. Account table: one row per account with product, tenure, contract start and end dates, region and channel of acquisition.
2. Billing history: twenty-four months of statements with amounts, discounts and any price changes.
3. Contact centre logs: call, chat and email contacts with reason codes and outcome codes.
4. Network quality: daily averages of line speed and outage minutes per exchange area.
5. Cancellation survey: free-text and multiple choice answers collected by the retention team at the point of cancellation, available for about 38 percent of leavers.

All data was pseudonymised before transfer. Postcodes were reduced to sector level and names, phone numbers and email addresses were removed. We stored the data in the Lumen secure workspace, with access limited to the two named analysts.

## 4. Data preparation

The largest task was linking billing history to contact logs, because the two systems used different account identifiers before the 2023 migration. Tidewell provided a mapping table, which matched 96.4 percent of accounts. The unmatched accounts were mostly very old accounts closed before the migration and were excluded from the modelling but kept in the descriptive figures.

We defined churn as an account that was closed by the customer, or ported out, within the period, excluding closures caused by home moves where the customer moved to an address outside the Tidewell network footprint. We also excluded closures for non-payment, which follow a separate collections process.

For each account and each month we built a feature set describing the previous ninety days: number and type of contacts, outage minutes, average line speed against the advertised speed, change in the bill compared with the previous quarter, months remaining on contract, whether a discount had recently ended, and product mix.

## 5. Descriptive findings

Churn was strongly linked to contract stage. Customers within their minimum term churned at 4.1 percent per year, mainly because of early termination charges. Customers in the three months after their minimum term ended churned at an annualised rate of 41 percent, falling to 22 percent for customers who had been out of contract for more than a year.

Product also mattered. Customers on copper broadband products churned at 23 percent per year against 12 percent for full fibre customers, even after accounting for region. Mobile-only customers churned less than broadband-only customers, and customers with both broadband and mobile churned least of all, at 9 percent.

Contact centre activity was a strong warning sign. Customers who contacted support three or more times in ninety days were more than twice as likely to leave in the next quarter. Repeated contacts about the same issue, particularly slow speeds and billing queries, were especially predictive.

Network quality had a smaller effect than the retention team expected. Outage minutes predicted churn only in exchange areas with more than six hours of outages per quarter, which affected less than 5 percent of customers.

## 6. Reasons given for leaving

We analysed 15,812 cancellation survey responses. The multiple choice answers were grouped into six categories, and we used topic modelling on the free-text comments to check and refine the categories.

The single most common reason, given by 46 percent of respondents, was an unexpected price increase at the end of the contract or at the annual price rise. Many comments mentioned that the new price was only discovered when the bill arrived, and that the new billing statements did not make the increase clear. This was by far the main driver of churn and it was much larger after the billing migration in 2023 than before it.

The second reason was a better offer from a competitor, mentioned by 21 percent, which often overlapped with the first reason. Slow or unreliable broadband was third at 14 percent. Poor customer service was mentioned by 9 percent, moving home within the footprint but choosing a new provider by 6 percent, and other reasons by 4 percent.

## 7. Predictive model

We trained a gradient boosted tree model to predict the probability that an active account will churn in the next ninety days. The model was trained on data from July 2022 to December 2023 and tested on January to June 2024. On the test period it achieved an area under the ROC curve of 0.81. The top decile of predicted risk contained 38 percent of all churners, compared with 10 percent if accounts were selected at random.

The most important features were months remaining on contract, the size of the most recent bill change, number of billing contacts in ninety days, product type and tenure. We produced explanations for each account so that retention advisers can see why an account is flagged, for example 'contract ended 2 months ago, bill rose 18 percent, 2 billing calls'.

We checked the model for unfair differences in performance across regions and acquisition channels and found no material gaps. We did not have access to age or other protected characteristics and did not attempt to infer them.

## 8. Financial impact

Using Tidewell's figures for average revenue per account and cost of acquiring a new customer, we estimate that each percentage point of churn reduction is worth about £1.1m per year in retained revenue. If the recommended actions reduce churn among out-of-contract customers by a fifth, overall churn would fall by roughly 1.8 points, worth about £2m per year before the cost of any discounts.

## 9. Recommendations

1. Communicate renewal prices clearly and early. Send a plain message 60 days before the end of the minimum term showing the current price, the new price, and the best available renewal offer side by side.
2. Redesign the bill so that any price change is shown at the top of the first page with the reason and the date it applies from.
3. Use the model each month to prioritise proactive retention calls for the top decile of risk, starting with customers who have had repeat billing contacts.
4. Offer full fibre upgrades to copper customers where available, at the same price for the first twelve months.
5. Introduce a 'fix it first time' target for repeat speed complaints, linked to engineer visits.

## 10. Proposed experiment

We recommend a randomised trial in Q4 2024 of recommendation 1. Out-of-contract customers would be randomly allocated to receive the new 60-day renewal message or the current standard letter. With about 18,000 customers reaching the end of their term each quarter, a three-month trial would detect a 3-point difference in churn with 80 percent power. The design document will be shared by 18 October.

## 11. Limitations

Survey responses were only available for about 38 percent of leavers, and those who answered may differ from those who did not. Contact reason codes are chosen by advisers and are not always consistent. The model will need retraining if Tidewell changes its pricing policy, because recent bill changes are such an important feature.

## Appendix A: Glossary

Churn: the share of accounts closed by customers in a period. Minimum term: the fixed period at the start of a contract during which early termination charges apply. Decile: one tenth of accounts ranked by predicted risk. ROC: receiver operating characteristic, a standard way of measuring how well a model separates two groups.

# Banana bread (Gran's version)

Makes one 900g loaf tin, about 10 slices.

## Ingredients
- 3 very ripe bananas, the blacker the better
- 75g melted butter, plus extra for greasing
- 150g light brown sugar
- 1 large egg, beaten
- 1 tsp vanilla extract
- 1 tsp bicarbonate of soda
- pinch of salt
- 190g plain flour
- 1 tsp ground cinnamon
- 60g chopped walnuts (optional)

## Method
1. Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan). Grease and line the loaf tin with baking parchment.
2. Mash the bananas in a large bowl with a fork until mostly smooth.
3. Stir in the melted butter, then the sugar, egg and vanilla.
4. Sprinkle over the bicarbonate of soda and salt, then fold in the flour and cinnamon until just combined. Do not overmix.
5. Fold in the walnuts and scrape the batter into the tin.
6. Bake for 55 to 65 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean. Cover with foil after 40 minutes if the top browns too quickly.
7. Cool in the tin for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a rack.

Notes: keeps for 4 days wrapped in foil. Freezes well in slices. Leo likes it with a few chocolate chips stirred in instead of walnuts.

# Chicken tikka masala

Serves 4. Marinate overnight if you can.

## Marinade
- 600g boneless chicken thighs, cut into chunks
- 150g plain yoghurt
- 1 tbsp lemon juice
- 2 tsp garam masala
- 1 tsp ground cumin
- 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
- 3 garlic cloves and a thumb of ginger, grated
- 1 tsp salt

## Sauce
- 2 tbsp oil and 20g butter
- 1 large onion, finely chopped
- 1 tbsp tomato puree
- 400g tin chopped tomatoes
- 1 tsp ground coriander, 1 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp garam masala
- 150ml double cream
- 1 tsp sugar
- handful of fresh coriander

## Method
1. Mix the marinade ingredients, coat the chicken and chill for at least 2 hours.
2. Thread onto skewers and grill on high for 10 to 12 minutes, turning, until charred at the edges.
3. Meanwhile fry the onion in oil and butter for 10 minutes until golden. Add the spices and tomato puree, cook for 1 minute, then add tomatoes and simmer 15 minutes.
4. Blend the sauce smooth, stir in the cream and sugar, add the grilled chicken and simmer 5 minutes.
5. Finish with coriander. Serve with basmati rice and naan.

- 4 eggs
- zest of 2 unwaxed lemons
- 225g self-raising flour
- 2 tbsp milk

```
npm install
```

# photo-renamer

A fast Rust command line utility that renames photos and videos using the date they were taken, so a folder of IMG_4821.JPG files becomes 2024-07-14_10-32-05.jpg.

## Install
```
cargo install --path .
```
Requires Rust 1.75 or newer.

## Usage
```
photo-renamer ~/Pictures/Camera --dry-run
photo-renamer ~/Pictures/Camera --pattern '{year}/{month}/{date}_{time}'
```

## How it works
- Reads EXIF DateTimeOriginal for JPEG and HEIC images
- Falls back to the QuickTime creation date for MOV and MP4 videos
- Uses the file modified time as a last resort and logs a warning
- Never overwrites: duplicates get a -1, -2 suffix

## Options
- --dry-run prints the plan without changing anything
- --undo restores names from the .renamer-log.json written in each folder
- --threads N controls parallelism (default: number of CPU cores)

## Development
cargo test runs unit tests with sample images in tests/data. Clippy must pass before merging.

Python scripts that save recipes from cooking websites as clean Markdown files, without ads and life stories, into Documents/Recipes.

```
source .venv/bin/activate
```

```
python scrape.py https://example.org/recipes/lemon-drizzle --out ~/Documents/Recipes
```

## How it works
1. Downloads the page and looks for schema.org Recipe JSON-LD data.
2. If found, extracts title, ingredients, method steps, servings and timings.
3. Otherwise falls back to heuristics based on common heading names.
4. Writes a Markdown file with an Ingredients list and a numbered Method.

## Notes
- Respect each site's terms and robots.txt; this is for personal use only.
- Unit conversion (cups to grams) is basic and lives in units.py.

# home-automation

Python services running on a Raspberry Pi 4 that tie together the smart plugs, the hallway temperature sensor and the weather dashboard.

## Components
- sensors/ reads the BME280 sensor over I2C every 60 seconds and stores readings in InfluxDB
- plugs/ controls Zigbee smart plugs through a Zigbee2MQTT bridge
- rules/ simple YAML automations, for example turning off the dehumidifier when humidity falls below 55 percent
- api/ a small FastAPI app that exposes current readings to the weather dashboard

## Requirements
- Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm
- Python 3.11, pip install -r requirements.txt
- Mosquitto MQTT broker

## Running
```
sudo systemctl enable --now home-sensors home-rules home-api
journalctl -u home-rules -f
```

## Safety
Never automate the heater plug without the thermal cut-out rule enabled. Rules are reloaded on SIGHUP.

## Ideas
- Notify my phone when the washing machine finishes (power draw drops below 5W)
- Log the fridge temperature during heatwaves

docs.name: Trip diary - Japan 2023.md
docs.body:
# Japan trip diary, April 2023

Daniel and I finally did it: two weeks in Japan for our fifth anniversary, with Leo staying at Grandma Rose's. I promised myself I would write something every evening, even if it was only a few lines. Here it is.

## Day 1 - Arrival in Tokyo

The overnight flight was long but I slept for almost six hours, which is a record for me. Landed at Haneda just after seven in the morning. Immigration was quick once we found the right queue and filled in the online form. We picked up our rail passes at the airport office and took the monorail into the city. The hotel in Asakusa let us leave our bags, so we walked around Senso-ji while it was still quiet. Daniel bought a fortune from the box at the temple and got 'bad luck', so he tied it to the rack and bought another one, which said 'small luck'. He was happy with that. We were asleep by eight.

## Day 2 - Tokyo

Jet lag woke us at four, so we went to the outer market at Tsukiji for breakfast. Tamagoyaki on a stick, grilled scallops, and the best tuna I have ever eaten. Then the long walk through Ginza, a coffee in a tiny shop where the owner ground each cup by hand, and the afternoon in the gardens at Hamarikyu. The tea house there serves matcha and a little sweet for a few hundred yen. In the evening we went up the tower at Shibuya for the view and walked across the famous crossing three times just because we could.

## Day 3 - Tokyo

Rain all day. We spent the morning in the digital art museum, which was much more fun than I expected. The room with the hanging lights made Daniel go quiet for once. Lunch was ramen at a counter where you order from a vending machine. In the afternoon we took the train to Shimokitazawa and went through vintage shops. I found a lovely indigo jacket. Dinner at an izakaya near the hotel, where the owner drew us a map to a bar that only seats six people.

## Day 4 - Day trip to Nikko

Early train to Nikko. The shrine complex is incredible, so much gold and carving, and the cedar avenue is beautiful in the mist. We walked up to the waterfall at Kegon, which was still half frozen. Daniel's knee started hurting on the stairs, so we took it slowly. Yuba, the tofu skin, is the local speciality; we had it in soup and in a kind of rolled sushi. Back in Tokyo late and very tired.

## Day 5 - Hakone

Travelled to Hakone on the romance car. The plan was to see Mount Fuji, but it hid behind clouds the whole day. We did the loop anyway: mountain railway, cable car, the ropeway over the volcanic valley where they sell black eggs boiled in the hot springs, and the pirate ship across the lake. Stayed in a small guesthouse with an outdoor bath. Sitting in hot water with cold air on your face is one of the best feelings in the world.

## Day 6 - Hakone to Kyoto

Woke up to a clear sky and there it was: Fuji, perfectly white, right outside the window. We almost missed the bus because we kept taking photos. Took the bullet train to Kyoto, sitting on the right side for one last look at the mountain.

In Kyoto we stayed four nights at Ryokan Hanamizuki, a family-run inn in a quiet lane near the Kamo river, about ten minutes on foot from Gion. Our room had tatami mats, sliding paper screens and a view of a tiny moss garden. The owner, Mrs Fujita, served a kaiseki dinner in the room on the first night, eleven courses, each one like a small painting. The futons were laid out while we were at the bath. I want to remember the name of this place forever, because it was the highlight of the whole trip.

## Day 7 - Kyoto

Up at six to beat the crowds at Fushimi Inari. We walked through the red gates almost to the top of the mountain and only met a handful of people until we came back down at nine, when it was packed. Breakfast of inari sushi from a stall. In the afternoon we visited Kiyomizu-dera and walked down the old stone lanes of Sannenzaka. The cherry blossoms were just past their peak, so the petals were falling like snow along the canal in the evening. Dinner was yakitori in Pontocho alley, sitting outside on a platform over the river.

## Day 8 - Kyoto

Arashiyama: the bamboo grove, which is smaller than the photos make it look but still magical in the early light, then the temple garden at Tenryu-ji and the monkey park on the hill. Daniel was nervous about the monkeys, which made me laugh. We rented bikes in the afternoon and cycled along the river. In the evening Mrs Fujita showed us how to wear yukata properly and we walked to Gion and saw two maiko hurrying to an appointment.

## Day 9 - Nara

Day trip to Nara. The deer bow to you if you bow first, and then try to eat your map. The Great Buddha hall is enormous. We had kakinoha sushi wrapped in persimmon leaves for lunch. Back in Kyoto I treated myself to a pair of handmade chopsticks with our names engraved.

## Day 10 - Kyoto to Osaka

Sad to leave the ryokan; Mrs Fujita gave us a small bag of sweets for the train and waved until we turned the corner. Osaka is louder, brighter and friendlier. We walked along Dotonbori under the giant crab and ate takoyaki and okonomiyaki until we could not move.

## Day 11 - Osaka and Himeji

Morning trip to Himeji castle, which is bright white and looks like a bird about to fly. Then back to Osaka for the aquarium, which has a whale shark in a tank that goes down several floors. Leo would love it. We bought him a plush whale shark.

## Day 12 - Hiroshima and Miyajima

A quiet, serious morning at the Peace Memorial Park and museum. I am glad we went, but it was hard. In the afternoon we took the ferry to Miyajima and saw the floating gate at high tide. Oysters grilled on the street, and maple-leaf cakes filled with custard.

## Day 13 - Back to Tokyo

Long train ride back to Tokyo. Last evening in Shinjuku, where we got lost in the station for twenty minutes, which apparently everyone does. Final dinner at a tempura counter where the chef fried each piece in front of us.

## Day 14 - Home

Packed everything into one extra bag we had to buy. Flight home in the afternoon. I already miss the trains, the convenience store sandwiches, the politeness, and most of all those four nights in Kyoto.

## Practical notes for next time

- The rail pass paid for itself with the bullet train trips to Kyoto, Hiroshima and back.
- A rechargeable transport card works on almost all local trains and in convenience stores.
- Carry cash: many small restaurants and the ryokan did not accept cards.
- Book popular restaurants and the digital art museum at least a month ahead.
- Pack slip-on shoes, because you take them off a lot.
- Total spent: about £4,600 for both of us, including flights and the rail pass.

## Budget breakdown

- Flights: £1,640 for two return tickets booked in November 2022
- Rail passes (14 days, ordinary class): £640 for both
- Hotels in Tokyo and Osaka: about £720
- Hakone guesthouse: £210 including dinner and breakfast
- Kyoto ryokan, four nights with two kaiseki dinners: £760
- Food, temples, museums and shopping: roughly £630

The ryokan was the biggest single cost but completely worth it. We booked it directly by email after reading about it in a travel forum, and Mrs Fujita replied within a day with directions drawn by hand.

## Things we would do differently

- Spend one less night in Tokyo and one more in Kyoto.
- Skip Nikko unless the weather is good, and go to Kamakura instead.
- Take smaller suitcases; the stairs at stations are hard work with big bags.
- Learn more basic phrases. People were incredibly patient, but I wanted to say more than thank you and excuse me.
- Bring a small towel and hand gel, as many public toilets have no paper towels.

## Souvenirs we bought

- For Leo: the plush whale shark, a bullet train model and a book of origami dinosaurs.
- For Grandma Rose: a furoshiki cloth with cherry blossom print.
- For Mrs Patel next door: matcha and a tin of rice crackers.
- For the office: a box of green tea Kit Kats, which vanished in ten minutes.

## Photo album plan

Print about sixty photos for an album, one page per day. Favourites: Fuji from the guesthouse window, the red gates at dawn, the moss garden at the ryokan, the deer in Nara, and Daniel in his yukata.

Brewmaster 300 Bean-to-Cup Coffee Machine
Quick start and care guide (extract)

1. Before first use
Rinse the water tank and fill to the MAX line with fresh cold water. Fill the bean hopper with whole beans, never ground coffee or flavoured beans. Press the power button and wait for the machine to heat and rinse automatically.

2. Brewing a drink
Press the single-cup or double-cup button. Turn the strength dial clockwise for a stronger flavour. For milk drinks, attach the milk tube to the frother and place it in a jug of cold milk.

3. Cleaning
Empty the drip tray and grounds container daily. Rinse the milk system after every use with the hot water button.

4. Descaling
When the orange descale light comes on, the machine needs descaling. In hard water areas this is about every 6 to 8 weeks.
- Remove the water filter cartridge.
- Mix one sachet of Brewmaster descaling solution with 500ml of water in the tank.
- Hold the descale and steam buttons together for 3 seconds. The cycle takes about 25 minutes and pauses halfway so you can empty the drip tray.
- Rinse the tank and run a second cycle with clean water only.
Do not use vinegar; it can damage the seals and void the warranty.

5. Troubleshooting
If coffee drips slowly, set the grinder one step coarser. A flashing red light means the grounds container is full or missing.

# Lecture 4: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
Module: ST7102 Statistical Inference, Dr Kowalczyk, 7 October 2024

## Key ideas
- Null hypothesis H0: no effect. Alternative H1: there is an effect.
- p-value: probability of seeing data at least as extreme as ours if H0 were true. It is not the probability that H0 is true.
- Significance level alpha, usually 0.05, fixed before seeing the data.
- Type I error: rejecting a true H0 (rate alpha). Type II error: failing to reject a false H0 (rate beta). Power = 1 - beta.

## Confidence intervals
- 95% CI for a mean: x-bar plus or minus t(0.975, n-1) times s divided by root n.
- Interpretation: if we repeated the study many times, 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true mean.
- CI and two-sided test agree: if the 95% CI excludes 0, p < 0.05.

## Power and sample size
- Power depends on effect size, variability, alpha and n.
- For comparing two proportions, use the normal approximation formula (see handout).

## Multiple testing
- Bonferroni: divide alpha by the number of tests. Conservative.
- Benjamini-Hochberg controls false discovery rate.

## Homework
Problem sheet 4, questions 1 to 6, due 14 October. Read chapter 6 of the course text.

docs.body:
# Chapter 3: Methodology
Draft 4, for supervisor review by Dr Kowalczyk. Thesis title: Predicting early disengagement from community food programmes in Ashbourne Vale.

## 3.1 Introduction

This chapter describes how the study was designed and carried out. It explains the research questions, the setting, the sources of data, how participants were recruited, the variables that were measured, the statistical methods used to answer each question, and the steps taken to ensure that the work was ethical and the results reliable. The aim is to give enough detail that another researcher could repeat the study in a similar setting and reach comparable conclusions.

The study uses a mixed approach. The main component is a prospective cohort study of households registering with three community food programmes over a twelve-month period, followed for six months after registration. A smaller qualitative component, based on semi-structured interviews with volunteers and programme coordinators, helps to interpret the quantitative findings and is reported in Chapter 5.

## 3.2 Research questions

The study addresses three questions.

RQ1. What proportion of households registering with a community food programme stop attending within the first three months, and how does this vary across programmes?

RQ2. Which characteristics of households and of their first contacts with the programme are associated with early disengagement?

RQ3. Can a simple risk score, based on information available at registration, identify households at high risk of disengagement well enough to be useful to coordinators?

## 3.3 Setting

The study took place in Ashbourne Vale, a town of about 85,000 people with a mix of suburban estates, an older town centre and surrounding villages. Three programmes agreed to take part: the Larkspur Community Pantry, a membership food club where households pay a small weekly fee for a basket of groceries; the St Brannoc Food Bank, which provides emergency parcels on referral; and the Quayside Community Kitchen, which offers a free cooked meal twice a week alongside advice sessions. The programmes differ in their model, opening hours and the support they offer, which allows comparison across settings.

## 3.4 Study design

A prospective cohort design was chosen because the research questions concern the timing of disengagement after first contact. A retrospective design using existing records was considered, but the records held by the programmes were incomplete and inconsistent, particularly for attendance after the first visit. By collecting data prospectively with a common form, it was possible to define attendance consistently across the three programmes.

The cohort was open: households joined the study at registration between 1 October 2023 and 30 September 2024, and each household was followed for 26 weeks from its registration date. The follow-up period therefore ended on 31 March 2025 for the last households to join.

## 3.5 Participants and recruitment

All adult household representatives registering with one of the three programmes during the recruitment period were eligible. Exclusion criteria were: being under 18; not being able to give informed consent; and registering only for a single emergency parcel with no intention of returning, as recorded by the referring agency.

At registration, volunteers explained the study using a plain-language information sheet, available in English, Polish, Urdu and Romanian. Households could take part in the study without any change to the service they received, and could withdraw at any time.

Of 538 households who registered during the recruitment period, 497 were eligible and 431 agreed to take part. Nineteen later withdrew consent or had no usable follow-up data, leaving a final sample of 412 households for analysis. This final sample size of 412 is the figure used in all models in Chapter 4. The participation rate among eligible households was therefore 82.9 percent, and the flow of participants is shown in Figure 3.1.

## 3.6 Sample size considerations

The planned sample size was based on RQ2. Pilot data from the Larkspur Community Pantry suggested that about 35 percent of households disengage within three months. With 400 households and an alpha of 0.05, the study would have 80 percent power to detect an odds ratio of 1.8 for a binary predictor present in 30 percent of households. The achieved sample of 412 therefore met the planned target. For RQ3, the rule of thumb of at least ten events per candidate predictor was applied; with about 140 expected events, no more than fourteen candidate predictors were included in the risk score development.

## 3.7 Measures

### Outcome

The primary outcome was early disengagement, defined as no attendance at the programme for at least six consecutive weeks starting within the first twelve weeks after registration, without a recorded reason such as moving away or no longer needing support. Attendance was recorded at every visit by volunteers using a tablet form linked to a pseudonymous household identifier.

### Predictors

Candidate predictors were chosen from the literature and from discussions with coordinators. They included: household size; presence of children under five; whether any adult was in paid employment; main source of income; travel time to the programme; whether the household had been referred by an agency or self-referred; dietary requirements; whether the first visit involved a wait of more than thirty minutes; and whether the household received any additional advice at the first visit, such as help with energy bills or benefits.

Travel time was calculated from the postcode sector of the household to the programme using public transport schedules, because many participants did not own a car.

## 3.8 Statistical analysis

For RQ1, the proportion of households disengaging within three months was estimated with 95 percent confidence intervals for each programme and overall. Time to disengagement was described with Kaplan-Meier curves, with households censored at the end of follow-up or when they left for a recorded reason.

For RQ2, a Cox proportional hazards model was fitted with time to disengagement as the outcome, including programme as a stratification variable. The proportional hazards assumption was checked with Schoenfeld residuals. As a sensitivity analysis, logistic regression was used with the binary three-month outcome.

For RQ3, a logistic regression risk score was developed using penalised estimation to reduce overfitting. Performance was assessed with the area under the ROC curve and calibration plots, and internal validation used 500 bootstrap samples to estimate optimism. A simplified points-based version of the score was also produced, so that coordinators could use it without software.

Missing data were handled with multiple imputation by chained equations, with twenty imputed datasets, under a missing-at-random assumption. Complete case analysis was carried out as a sensitivity check.

All analyses were carried out in R version 4.3 using the survival, mice and rms packages. Code is stored in a private repository and will be made available on request.

## 3.9 Qualitative component

Twelve semi-structured interviews were carried out with volunteers and coordinators, four from each programme, between May and July 2024. Interviews lasted between 35 and 60 minutes, were recorded with consent and transcribed. Thematic analysis followed a six-phase approach, with an initial coding frame developed from the research questions and refined as new themes emerged.

## 3.10 Ethics

Ethical approval was granted by the University of Northmoor School of Mathematics Research Ethics Committee, reference SMREC-2023-118, on 14 September 2023. Data were pseudonymised at the point of collection and stored on university-managed encrypted storage. No names or full addresses were collected. Households were told that taking part would not affect the support they received. Volunteers who collected data received a short training session on consent and data protection.

## 3.11 Reflexivity

I volunteered at the Larkspur Community Pantry for two years before starting this research. This gave me useful knowledge of how the programmes operate and helped build trust, but it also brought a risk that I would interpret findings in a way that favoured that programme. To reduce this risk, a second coder from outside the programmes coded a quarter of the interview transcripts, and the coding frame was discussed with my supervisor.

## 3.12 Limitations of the design

The study took place in one town and the findings may not apply elsewhere. Attendance recording depended on volunteers and may have missed some visits. The definition of disengagement is necessarily somewhat arbitrary, and results using an eight-week definition are reported in the appendix. Finally, households who declined to take part may differ from participants in ways that could bias the estimates.

## 3.13 Summary

This chapter has set out a prospective cohort design with a final sample of 412 households from three programmes, a clear definition of early disengagement, and a set of statistical methods matched to each research question. The next chapter presents the results.

Notes for myself: check that Figure 3.1 numbers match the text; ask Dr Kowalczyk whether the eight-week sensitivity analysis belongs in the main text; add citation for the events-per-variable rule.

## Appendix to Chapter 3: Data collection form fields

The registration form recorded the household identifier, programme, date of registration, household size, number of children under five, employment status of each adult, main income source, referral route, dietary requirements, waiting time at the first visit, and any advice provided. The attendance form recorded the household identifier, date, programme, and type of support received at each visit. Volunteers were asked to record visits on the same day, and coordinators reviewed the forms each week for missing entries. Where a visit was recorded twice, the duplicate was removed before analysis, and any household with no attendance recorded after registration was contacted once by the coordinator to confirm whether they had moved away.

# Annual performance and development review, 2024
Employee: Maya Collins, Senior Data Analyst, Insights and Data Science
Reviewer: Priya Nandakumar, Head of Insights
Review period: 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2024 (mid-cycle check-in held 3 July)
Meeting date: 13 November 2024

## Part 1: Purpose of this review

The annual review is a chance to look back on the year, recognise achievements, agree areas for development, and set objectives for the coming year. It is a two-way conversation. Both the employee and the reviewer complete their sections before the meeting, and the final document is agreed and signed by both. Ratings feed into the annual pay review in April but are not the only factor considered.

The Lumen Analytics competency framework has five areas: technical excellence, client impact, collaboration, communication, and leadership. Each area is rated on a four-point scale: developing, solid, strong, and exceptional.

## Part 2: Employee self-assessment

### What went well this year

This year my biggest piece of work was the Tidewell Telecom churn analysis. I led it from scoping through to the final report, working with Owen on the modelling and with the client's retention and billing teams. The report identified unexpected price increases at renewal as the main driver of churn and the client has agreed to run a renewal messaging experiment in Q4, which I am designing.

I also built and launched the self-serve reporting suite, which is now used by about 140 people across three clients and internally. I ran four training sessions on it and wrote the help pages.

In the second half of the year I started the Brackenford Housing Association discovery project and I am mentoring two graduate analysts, Ben and Farah. Both have taken on more independent work since the summer.

Outside client work, I joined the interview panel for graduate hiring and helped redesign the technical exercise so that it is fairer for candidates without a computer science degree.

### What was challenging

The Tidewell project was delivered two weeks later than planned because data access took longer than expected. I should have escalated sooner instead of trying to work around the delays. I also found it hard to balance mentoring with delivery during August and September, when both projects were busy at the same time.

I am also still working on my MSc thesis part time, which has meant some long evenings, especially around the data collection deadline in September.

### What I want to develop

I would like to become more confident leading conversations with senior client stakeholders without Priya in the room, and to build more experience with experiment design and causal inference. Longer term I am interested in a principal analyst role.

## Part 3: Reviewer assessment

### Technical excellence: Strong

Maya's technical work is consistently careful and well documented. The churn model was well validated, with clear explanations at account level, which is exactly what the client's retention advisers needed. Her code is readable and she has started contributing to our shared internal libraries. To move to exceptional, I would like to see Maya go deeper into experimental methods, which fits well with the Tidewell trial.

### Client impact: Exceptional

The Tidewell findings have had a real effect on the client's pricing strategy, and their Commercial Director mentioned Maya by name in our quarterly account review. The reporting suite is one of our most valued deliverables. Brackenford have said the discovery interviews were the most useful they have taken part in.

### Collaboration: Strong

Maya is generous with her time and colleagues regularly come to her with questions. Owen described working with her as the best project experience he has had at Lumen. Her contribution to the hiring panel was valuable.

### Communication: Strong

Maya writes clear reports and her slides are simple and focused. At the start of the year she was nervous presenting to larger groups and tended to read from her notes. Since the spring her presentations have improved noticeably. Her Tidewell readout to the client's board in September was confident and well paced, she handled difficult questions about the model calmly, and several attendees commented on how easy it was to follow. I would now like Maya to present at the company all-hands at least once in the next year, and to take the lead in at least two client steering meetings without me. I have also put her forward for the external presentation skills course in February so she can build on this progress.

### Leadership: Solid

Maya's mentoring of Ben and Farah has been effective, and both now run their own analyses with much less support. The main area for growth is planning and escalation: the Tidewell delay could have been reduced by raising the data access issue with me a few weeks earlier. I would like Maya to use the project risk log consistently and raise blockers in our weekly check-in.

### Overall rating: Strong, with exceptional client impact

## Part 4: Objectives for 2025

1. Design, launch and analyse the Tidewell renewal messaging experiment, with a readout to the client by the end of Q1 2025.
2. Lead the Brackenford Housing Association modelling phase, including the risk log and weekly status updates.
3. Present at one company all-hands and lead two client steering meetings independently.
4. Complete the external presentation skills course and the internal causal inference workshop.
5. Continue mentoring Ben and Farah, and take on the new graduate starting in January.
6. Submit the MSc thesis by the agreed deadline, with study leave of five days to be booked in advance.

## Part 5: Wellbeing and workload

We discussed workload during the late summer and agreed that Maya will flag early if two projects overlap at peak times. Maya confirmed she is happy with her hybrid working pattern of two office days. Priya reminded Maya that she has eight days of annual leave left and should book them before the end of the year, as only five days can be carried over.

## Part 6: Career conversation

Maya is interested in the principal analyst track. Priya explained that this usually requires two consecutive years of strong or exceptional ratings, evidence of leading larger projects, and a contribution to the wider practice, such as internal training or publications. Maya's trajectory is on track for a promotion conversation in the 2025 review if the objectives above are met. Priya will arrange for Maya to shadow Grace Ilori, a principal analyst, on a client pitch in the new year.

## Part 7: Training and support agreed

- External presentation skills course, two days, February 2025, budget approved
- Internal causal inference workshop, March 2025
- Five days of study leave for the MSc thesis
- Monthly one-to-one with Priya focused on stakeholder management

## Part 8: Employee comments

I think this is a fair review and I am grateful for the feedback on presenting, which has been something I worked hard on this year. I agree with the point on escalation. I am looking forward to the experiment work.

Signed: Maya Collins, 15 November 2024
Signed: Priya Nandakumar, 15 November 2024

Next step: ratings go to the calibration panel on 2 December; pay review outcome letters are issued in March.

## Appendix: Feedback gathered from colleagues

As part of the review, Priya collected short written comments from four colleagues who worked closely with Maya this year.

Owen Pike, Analyst: Maya is the most organised person I have worked with on a project. She explains why we are doing something, not just what to do. She sometimes takes on too much herself rather than asking for help.

Ben Ashdown, Graduate Analyst: Maya's code reviews are detailed but always encouraging. I learned more from our weekly pairing sessions than from any course. It would help if she shared her project plans earlier so I can plan my own time.

Farah Qureshi, Graduate Analyst: She made me feel welcome from my first day. Her explanation of survival models finally made sense to me. I would like more chances to present our work to clients alongside her.

Gail Rennick, Brackenford Housing Association (client): The discovery interviews were thoughtful and the summary was the clearest document we have received from any supplier. Maya listened to our repair coordinators and did not assume she knew the answers.

## Appendix: Objectives from 2024 and outcomes

1. Deliver the Tidewell churn analysis: achieved, two weeks late.
2. Launch the self-serve reporting suite: achieved, adoption above target.
3. Mentor one graduate analyst: exceeded, mentoring two.
4. Complete the MSc data collection: achieved in September.
5. Improve confidence presenting to large groups: achieved, as noted above.

Calibration note from the People Team: ratings for the Insights team were reviewed alongside the Engineering and Client Services teams to make sure the scale is applied consistently. Maya's overall rating was confirmed without change. Any questions about the process can be raised with Tom Elridge, Head of People, before the pay review letters are issued in March. Development plans agreed in this review should be uploaded to the HR portal by 20 December so the training budget can be reserved.

docs.body:
# Dal tadka (yellow lentil dal)

Serves 4. From Priya at university, adjusted for our spice tolerance.

## Dal
- 200g toor dal (split pigeon peas) or yellow moong dal, rinsed until the water runs clear
- 900ml water
- 1/2 tsp turmeric
- 1 tsp salt
- 1 tomato, chopped

## Tadka (tempering)
- 2 tbsp ghee or oil
- 1 tsp cumin seeds
- 1/2 tsp mustard seeds
- pinch of asafoetida (hing)
- 2 dried red chillies
- 4 garlic cloves, sliced
- 1 onion, finely chopped
- 1 green chilli, slit
- 1 tsp grated ginger
- 1/2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
- 1/2 tsp garam masala
- fresh coriander and a squeeze of lemon

## Method
1. Pressure cook the dal with water, turmeric and salt for 3 whistles, or simmer in a pan for 35 to 40 minutes, until soft. Whisk smooth and add the tomato.
2. Heat ghee, add cumin and mustard seeds until they crackle, then hing, dried chillies and garlic until golden.
3. Add onion, green chilli and ginger and fry until soft. Add chilli powder and garam masala.
4. Pour the sizzling tadka over the dal. Finish with coriander and lemon.

Serve with jeera rice or rotis.

# Lumen Analytics Ltd - Employee Handbook
Version 2024.2, issued by the People Team. This handbook applies to all employees in the United Kingdom and should be read together with your contract of employment.

## 1. Welcome

Welcome to Lumen Analytics. We are a team of around 120 analysts, data scientists, engineers and support staff helping organisations make better decisions with their data. This handbook explains how we work, what you can expect from us, and what we expect from you. Where this handbook and your contract differ, your contract takes priority. Policies are reviewed every year and the latest version is always on the intranet.

## 2. Our values

We are curious: we ask good questions before we look for answers. We are careful: we check our work and we are honest about uncertainty. We are kind: we treat colleagues, clients and the people in our data with respect. We are open: we share what we learn and we admit mistakes early.

## 3. Working hours and hybrid working

Standard full-time hours are 37.5 per week, normally between 8am and 6pm with an hour for lunch. Core collaboration hours are 10am to 4pm, Monday to Thursday. Most roles are hybrid, with two days a week in the Ashbourne Vale office. Teams agree their office days together. If you would like to work a different pattern, including part-time or compressed hours, you can make a flexible working request from your first day of employment. We will respond within two months.

You may work from another country for up to 20 working days a year with approval from your manager and the People Team, so that we can check tax and data protection rules.

## 4. Pay and expenses

Salaries are paid monthly on the last working day, by bank transfer. Pay is reviewed every April, taking into account performance, market data and the company's results. Expenses for client travel, approved training and equipment must be claimed through the expenses system within 60 days, with receipts. Train travel should be standard class; flights only for journeys over four hours by rail. The home working allowance is a one-off £300 for new starters to buy a chair, desk or other equipment.

## 5. Pension and benefits

You will be enrolled in the Lumen Analytics Group Personal Pension with Evergreen Retirement Trust. The standard arrangement is a 5 percent employee contribution through salary sacrifice and a 6 percent employer contribution. Other benefits include private medical insurance with Meridale Health after probation, life assurance at four times salary, an employee assistance programme, a cycle to work scheme, an eye test voucher, and a yearly learning budget of £1,000 per person.

## 6. Holidays and time off

The holiday year runs from 1 January to 31 December. Full-time employees are entitled to 25 days of annual leave each year, plus the eight UK bank holidays. After three years of continuous service this rises to 27 days, and after five years to 28 days. Part-time employees receive a pro rata entitlement. In your first and last year, entitlement is calculated in proportion to the part of the year you work.

Please book leave through the HR portal at least two weeks in advance for absences of three days or more, and agree dates with your team so client work is covered. You may carry over up to five unused days into the next holiday year, to be used by 31 March. Unused days above this are lost unless there are exceptional circumstances, such as long-term sickness or parental leave.

The office closes between Christmas and New Year, and employees are asked to keep three days of their annual leave for this period.

You can also buy up to five extra days of holiday a year through salary sacrifice in the January benefits window.

Other time off includes: up to two days of paid compassionate leave for a close family bereavement, extendable at your manager's discretion; one paid volunteering day a year; reasonable unpaid time off for dependants in an emergency; and paid time off for jury service, topped up to full pay.

## 7. Sickness absence

If you are unwell and cannot work, tell your manager by 9:30am on the first day, by phone or message. For absences of more than seven calendar days, you will need a fit note from a doctor. Company sick pay is full pay for up to eight weeks in any rolling twelve months after probation, then statutory sick pay. We may arrange a return-to-work conversation and occupational health support where helpful.

## 8. Family leave

Enhanced maternity and adoption pay is 20 weeks at full pay followed by 6 weeks at half pay, then statutory pay. Paternity and partner leave is 6 weeks at full pay, which can be taken in blocks within the first year. Shared parental leave is enhanced in line with maternity pay. Parents may also take up to 18 weeks of unpaid parental leave per child before the child's eighteenth birthday.

## 9. Learning and development

Each employee has an annual learning budget of £1,000 and five days of learning time. Use it for courses, conferences, books or certifications related to your role. Study leave for a relevant degree may be agreed separately with your manager. We run a monthly internal seminar series and an annual hackathon.

## 10. Performance and reviews

We hold a mid-year check-in in July and an annual review in November. Reviews use the competency framework of technical excellence, client impact, collaboration, communication and leadership. Ratings are calibrated across teams before pay decisions are made.

## 11. Conduct

We expect everyone to behave professionally and respectfully. Bullying, harassment and discrimination are not tolerated. Concerns can be raised with your manager, the People Team, or anonymously through the whistleblowing line. Conflicts of interest, including freelance work for clients or competitors, must be declared. Freelance work that does not compete with Lumen is generally allowed if declared in advance.

## 12. Data protection and security

Client data must only be stored in approved secure workspaces. Never download client data to personal devices, never email unencrypted data extracts, and lock your screen when you step away. Report suspected incidents to the security team within one hour. Completing the annual security training is mandatory.

## 13. Equipment

You will receive a company laptop and accessories. Lost or stolen equipment must be reported immediately. Personal use should be light and reasonable. Return all equipment on your last day.

## 14. Notice periods and leaving

Notice is one month during probation and two months after, unless your contract says otherwise. Untaken holiday will be paid in your final salary, and any holiday taken beyond your pro rata entitlement will be deducted. We hold exit interviews to learn from your experience.

## 15. Contacts

People Team: people@lumen-analytics.example. IT help desk: ext 400. Security: security@lumen-analytics.example. Employee assistance programme: available 24 hours, details on the intranet.

## 16. Travel and client visits

When visiting client sites, follow the client's own safety and security rules, wear your Lumen badge, and never leave laptops in cars. Book travel through the travel portal so that we know where you are in an emergency. Mileage for using your own car on business is reimbursed at 45p per mile for the first 10,000 miles in the tax year. Travel between home and the Ashbourne Vale office is not a business journey.

## 17. Health, safety and wellbeing

All employees should complete a display screen equipment assessment within their first month, for both the office and home workspace. Report any accident or near miss to the office manager. Mental health first aiders are listed on the intranet, and you can speak to them in confidence. The employee assistance programme offers up to six free counselling sessions a year.

## 18. Social media and public speaking

You are welcome to talk about your work at conferences and online, but please do not share client names or data without written permission. If you are invited to speak at an event as a Lumen representative, let the marketing team know so they can help with slides and promotion.

## 19. Grievances and disciplinary matters

If you have a concern about your work, try to resolve it informally with your manager first. If that does not work, you can raise a formal grievance in writing with the People Team, and we will arrange a meeting within ten working days. You have the right to be accompanied by a colleague or trade union representative at formal meetings. Our disciplinary procedure follows the ACAS code of practice.

## 20. Changes to this handbook

We may update this handbook from time to time. We will tell you about significant changes by email and on the intranet at least one month before they take effect.

- Carry over: up to 5 days, use by 31 March
